title: The divine eye
hookLine: after a week of hearing, Arjuna asks to see God's real form and is told his eyes won't do; why Hindus go for darshan
carry: darshan: the sight of God is a gift

cards: Ten chapters on a chariot, and Arjuna has heard it all.
This week alone: Sudama's rice; chores offered like the milkmaids' churning; the robber who became a poet; the lotus with no bottom; where to look; the taste in water. He believes every word.
But hearing about someone you love isn't the same as seeing them. So the warrior turns to his friend and asks for the one thing words can't give.

teach.b: Verse one: out of kindness to me you've told me this highest secret about the self, and my confusion is gone. Verse two: I've heard in detail how beings come and go, and about your greatness that doesn't end.
Verse three: it is just as you say. But I want to see it: your form as the Lord of all.

teach.h: IF YOU THINK I'M ABLE, SHOW ME.
teach.b: Then verse four, a lovely bit of humility: if you think I'm able to see it, master of yoga, show me your imperishable self. If you think I'm able. He doesn't demand.
He asks, and leaves room for no. Krishna says yes. Verse five: behold my forms, by hundreds and thousands, divine, of many colors and shapes.

Verse six: see the gods of the sky and the storm, wonders no one has seen before. Verse seven: see the whole universe, moving and unmoving, gathered here in my body, and anything else you want to see.
Then the catch, verse eight: you can't see me with these eyes of yours, so I give you a divine eye. Divyam chakshuh. Behold my power.
That's the key to the whole chapter. Seeing God isn't a matter of looking harder with ordinary eyes; the sight itself has to be given.

In the Mahabharata, the narrator Sanjaya, telling all this to the blind king, has been given a divine eye too, so he can see the battlefield from the palace. That's how anyone hearing the story gets to watch.
Many Hindus hear the same idea in darshan at the temple: seeing God and being seen, a sight received, not taken.

how: Many Hindus speak of darshan, seeing and being seen by the divine, when they visit a temple; chapter eleven, where Arjuna asks to see and is given a divine eye, is often read as the Gita's great darshan.

o: a divine eye, sight that's given
a third eye opened by long study

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.
p: if you think I'm able, show me
the whole universe in my body

s: Arjuna demands that Krishna prove himself
verse 4: if you think I'm able to see it, show me. he asks, and leaves room for no.
Krishna says ordinary eyes can't see his cosmic form
verse 8: you can't see me with these eyes, so I give you a divine eye.
the narrator of the Gita watches the battle in person
Sanjaya tells it to the blind king from the palace, by a divine sight he's been given.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you've heard everything, and you want to see God's true form. how do you ask?
o: prove it, or I won't fight.
if you think I'm able, show me.
I'll look harder until I see.
games.why: if you think I'm able, show me. and Krishna answers with a gift: a divine eye, since ordinary eyes can't see it.

practice: Close your eyes and notice that everything you usually look at is gone, yet something is still seeing: shapes, colors, the dark behind the lids. Rest in that.
Then think of one thing, or one person, you'd like to see more truly, and without forcing anything, ask in your own way, as Arjuna did: if I'm able, show me.

wordCard.voice: Divyam chakshuh. A divine eye. After hearing, Arjuna asks for sight, and Krishna gives him this eye, because ordinary eyes can't see it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: divyam chakshuh, a divine eye (11.8); chakshuh, the eye, the power of seeing.

carryVoice: Your line: darshan, the sight of God is a gift. Arjuna asked, and left room for no. A whole week, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 11.5–11.8 (behold my forms; a divine eye)
Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (Vyasa grants Sanjaya divine sight)
